content: Recency testing is a critical tool for managing individuals with HIV or their partners. The 204 Consolidated Guidelines on person-centered HIV strategic information emphasize the importance of using multiple test results to meet the requirements of a Recent Infection Testing Algorithm (RITA). When calculating recency proportions, it is essential to carefully consider the denominators used and account for variations in testing rates across different population groups or over time. The utility of recency assays in describing the distribution and trends of recent infections should be compared with other direct and indirect surveillance methods for estimating HIV incidence. Routine antenatal HIV testing has been a cornerstone of HIV surveillance since the early days of the global HIV/AIDS pandemic. Pregnant women attending antenatal care (ANC) were identified as an ideal sentinel population for monitoring population-wide HIV trends. This is because women typically become pregnant and seek health screening at ANC for reasons unrelated to HIV risk factors or disease. Consequently, HIV prevalence among pregnant women was considered more representative of population-wide HIV levels than prevalence among other sentinel populations, such as clients at STI clinics or hospital inpatients, who are disproportionately affected by HIV/AIDS. Following evidence of the effectiveness of antiretroviral drugs (ARVs) in preventing mother-to-child transmission of HIV and WHO recommendations for universal treatment, HIV testing at the first ANC visit has become nearly universal in most countries heavily affected by HIV. Many countries now follow WHO guidelines to retest women at the final ANC visit or during labor and delivery to identify any seroconversions since the initial screening. Routine reporting of aggregate outcomes typically includes the number of new clients attending their first ANC visit during a current pregnancy, the number of ANC clients already diagnosed with HIV and therefore not tested, the number of ANC clients tested for HIV, the number of ANC clients who tested HIV-positive, the number already on lifelong ART prior to the first ANC visit, and the number of HIV-positive ANC clients who initiated ART during ANC. When ANC attendance rates and HIV testing coverage are high, and data are robustly recorded, these indicators provide valuable insights into the epidemic. These data elements measure HIV testing coverage at ANC, HIV prevalence among pregnant women attending ANC, and ART coverage prior to the first ANC visit. Estimates of HIV prevalence among pregnant women attending ANC must account for women already known to be HIV-positive separately from new HIV diagnoses. Using routine ANC HIV testing data instead of sentinel surveillance data addresses the lack of representativeness in site selection that previously hindered the interpretation of ANC sentinel surveillance. Routine ANC testing data offer several advantages over ANC sentinel surveys. First, routine reporting for monitoring HIV service delivery reduces the cost and complexity of implementing bespoke survey activities. Second, any surveillance budget spent on improving these data ultimately enhances services for pregnant women. Third, data are available for nearly all pregnant women, providing granular spatial and temporal information. However, limitations exist when using routine ANC testing data for surveillance. These data may be subject to biases due to incomplete testing of all pregnant women, changes in testing policy, test kit availability, incomplete reporting by some facilities, or reporting errors. Even modest but systematic reporting errors can bias HIV incidence estimates. It is crucial to determine whether observed trends and patterns among routine ANC testing reflect true epidemiologic changes in HIV among pregnant women rather than changes in HIV testing or reporting practices. To address these limitations, combining routine reporting of ANC testing with regular and systematically sampled data quality assurance can provide more robust data for HIV surveillance. Relating HIV prevalence among pregnant women to population HIV prevalence requires accounting for systematic differences between pregnant women and the general population. For example, in mature epidemics, HIV prevalence tends to be lower among pregnant women over age 20 than among non-pregnant women, with the relative difference increasing with age. In contrast, pregnant adolescents aged 15–19 years tend to have higher HIV prevalence than non-pregnant adolescents. Lower HIV prevalence among pregnant women over age 20 has been linked to biological, behavioral, and structural factors, including reduced fecundity, higher rates of fetal loss, increased risk of widowhood and divorce, lower coital frequency, higher secondary abstinence, and structural differences such as higher HIV prevalence among urban populations with lower fertility. As HIV incidence declines over time and prevalence shifts to older ages, HIV prevalence among pregnant women may decline more rapidly than in the general adult population. Failing to account for this may overstate the level of HIV epidemic decline inferred from routine ANC testing. Age-standardizing observed ANC prevalence data partially, but not fully, accounts for differences in prevalence levels and trends among ANC clients compared with the general population. ART availability may reduce fertility differences between HIV-positive and HIV-negative women. Effective ART may ameliorate reduced fecundity of HIV-positive women, reduce widowhood, increase exposure to pregnancy, and reduce barriers to achieving desired family size. Monitoring fertility among women on ART is important for interpreting trends in ANC prevalence to monitor population HIV trends. Although data were deemed insufficient, a 2016 systematic review suggested that fertility among women on ART was likely higher than untreated HIV-positive women but lower than HIV-negative women. Data from Western Cape Province in South Africa identified substantially higher pregnancy rates among women on ART. The robustness of routine ANC testing data for surveillance depends on several conditions. ANC attendance must be high, and all women should be recorded, including those attending private-sector ANC services. HIV testing should be offered to all pregnant women and not restricted to higher-risk women or interrupted due to stock-outs of test kits. Only the first HIV test result should be used to calculate HIV prevalence during a single pregnancy. Women already known to be HIV-positive and/or on ART prior to their first ANC visit should be recorded and included in routine reporting. All HIV-positive women must be included in both the numerator and denominator when calculating HIV prevalence among pregnant women. These conditions should be verified through auditing ANC testing and reporting guidelines, reporting systems, registers, and data capture forms. Constructing ANC testing cascades can help review the internal consistency of reported data. Consistency checks include ensuring the number of ANC clients is similar to the expected number of births, the number of pregnant women with ascertained HIV status is similar to the number of ANC clients, and the number of pregnant women already on ART is less than the number known to be HIV-positive prior to the first ANC visit. For surveillance purposes, each ANC HIV test and its result should be recorded separately to distinguish a woman’s first HIV test during pregnancy from retesting during labor and delivery. If retesting results are included with first ANC HIV test results, this can bias HIV prevalence estimates downward and exaggerate apparent declines in prevalence. Reviewing retesting data as part of ANC testing cascade analyses can confirm whether data conform to HIV program implementation and verify that retesting data were not inadvertently reported as part of first ANC HIV test outcomes. Routine ANC HIV testing data can also be used to estimate HIV incidence. Mathematical models, such as the UNAIDS-supported Estimation and Projection Package (EPP) in the Spectrum model, have been used to estimate HIV incidence and prevalence trends among ANC attendees. These models account for systematic differences between prevalence in the ANC population and the general population. However, direct incidence estimation using ANC retesting data should be interpreted cautiously due to potential biases, such as misclassification of HIV-positive women as HIV-negative at their first ANC visit.
